subject: history
title: The Cultural Revolution (1966–1976)
dek: In May 1966 Mao Zedong launched a campaign he called the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution. Students and workers formed Red Guards, attacked party officials and intellectuals, and fought each other in the streets. The party-state nearly collapsed, millions of urban youths were sent to the countryside, Mao's chosen successor died fleeing the country, and the decade ended only after Mao's death and the arrest of the Gang of Four. Historians still argue about the death toll, but most serious estimates for the first five years alone run into the hundreds of thousands or more than a million.
honesty: The Cultural Revolution is still politically sensitive in China, and many local archives remain closed, so numbers and motives are contested. Death-toll estimates vary widely. This lesson uses the range derived by Andrew Walder and Yang Su from thousands of county and city annals: about 1.1 to 1.6 million deaths in 1966–1971, with most deaths caused by repression after the army restored order rather than by Red Guard street fighting. Higher figures exist in older secondary sources; treat them as speculative. The movement's official end is dated to the arrest of the Gang of Four on 6 October 1976, though the Communist Party later fixed its verdict in 1981. Personal stories of persecution are better documented for cities than for the countryside. There are no images today rather than risk pictures that do not match their captions.

timeline.label: Great Leap Forward and famine
timeline.detail: Mao's crash industrialisation and collectivisation campaign fails. Tens of millions die in the resulting famine. Mao is forced to retreat from day-to-day economic management, and Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping take charge of recovery.

timeline.label: Two lines harden
timeline.detail: Liu and Deng restore incentives and expertise. Mao warns that the party itself may be taking a capitalist road. Lin Biao, defence minister, pushes study of Mao's writings inside the army.

timeline.label: Quotations from Chairman Mao
timeline.detail: The People's Liberation Army publishes the first edition of Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung, later nicknamed the Little Red Book, for internal military use.

timeline.label: The May 16 Notification
timeline.detail: An expanded Politburo meeting issues a Central Committee circular warning that bourgeois representatives have infiltrated the party, government and army. The Five Man Group is dissolved and a new Cultural Revolution Group is created under Chen Boda, with Jiang Qing as a leading member.

timeline.label: Big-character poster at Peking University
timeline.detail: Nie Yuanzi and six others put up a dazibao attacking the university party committee. Mao orders it broadcast nationwide. Student activism spreads.

timeline.label: "Bombard the Headquarters"
timeline.detail: Mao writes his own big-character poster attacking the "bourgeois dictatorship" inside the party. The Eleventh Plenum elevates Lin Biao and sidelines Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping.

timeline.label: Red August
timeline.detail: Mao reviews millions of Red Guards in Tiananmen Square. In Beijing, Red Guards beat and kill teachers and other "class enemies", smash temples and shops labelled as the Four Olds, and force families with bad class labels from the city.

timeline.label: Shanghai January Storm
timeline.detail: Rebel workers and radicals overthrow the municipal party apparatus in Shanghai. Similar power seizures follow in other cities. Revolutionary committees replace old party committees, then split into armed factions.

timeline.label: Army restores order
timeline.detail: Factional fighting escalates. Mao orders the People's Liberation Army to intervene. By late 1968 most Red Guard organisations are disbanded.

timeline.label: Down to the countryside
timeline.detail: The campaign "Up to the Mountains and Down to the Countryside" sends roughly 17 million urban youths to rural areas for re-education through labour. Many stay for years.

timeline.label: Ninth Party Congress
timeline.detail: A new party constitution names Lin Biao as Mao's "close comrade-in-arms and successor".

timeline.label: Lin Biao's plane crashes
timeline.detail: After a failed plot and a break with Mao, Lin Biao, his wife Ye Qun and their son Lin Liguo die when their plane crashes in Mongolia while fleeing toward the Soviet Union. The official story calls it a coup attempt.

timeline.label: Nixon visits China
timeline.detail: U.S. President Richard Nixon meets Mao and Zhou Enlai in Beijing, opening a strategic turn against the Soviet Union while the Cultural Revolution continues at home.

timeline.label: Zhou Enlai dies
timeline.detail: Premier Zhou Enlai dies of cancer. Mourning for him becomes a channel for public anger at radical leaders.

timeline.label: Tiananmen mourning protests
timeline.detail: Crowds gather in Tiananmen Square around wreaths for Zhou. The Politburo clears the square, blames Deng Xiaoping, and strips him of his posts again.

timeline.label: Mao dies
timeline.detail: Mao Zedong dies. Hua Guofeng is already premier and first vice chairman.

timeline.label: Gang of Four arrested
timeline.detail: Hua Guofeng and military leaders arrest Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen. The Cultural Revolution is treated as over.

timeline.label: Party verdict
timeline.detail: The Communist Party's Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party since the Founding of the People's Republic of China condemns the Cultural Revolution as a catastrophe for which Mao bears chief responsibility, while keeping Mao's overall historical role as largely positive.

sections.title: A failed leap, a damaged chairman, and a party that no longer obeyed him

blocks.text: By the mid-1960s the People's Republic of China was seventeen years old. Mao Zedong had led the Communist Party to victory in 1949, remade land ownership, fought the United States to a stalemate in Korea, and built a one-party state. He was still the party's chairman. But his authority inside the leadership had been damaged by the disaster of the Great Leap Forward.

Between 1958 and 1962 Mao drove China into a crash programme of backyard steel furnaces, people's communes and exaggerated grain targets. The result was famine. Demographic studies put excess deaths in the tens of millions. Mao's colleagues forced him to step back from day-to-day economic work. State President Liu Shaoqi and General Secretary Deng Xiaoping ran the recovery: they restored private plots, brought back technical experts, and emphasised production over political campaigns.

Mao did not accept that retreat as final. He feared that the Soviet Union under Nikita Khrushchev had become "revisionist" — socialist in name, capitalist in practice — and that China might follow. In 1962 he told a party conference that class struggle continued under socialism and that the bourgeoisie might reappear inside the Communist Party itself. Defence Minister Lin Biao turned the army into a school of Mao Zedong Thought. From May 1964 the People's Liberation Army circulated a pocket anthology, Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung, later printed in hundreds of millions of red vinyl copies.

By early 1966 Mao had decided that culture and education were controlled by people who did not share his line, and that the party apparatus under Liu and Deng was blocking him. The campaign that followed was not a spontaneous student revolt that Mao then joined. It was a power struggle he started from the top, using students, workers and the army as instruments against his own party.

sections.title: What "Cultural Revolution" was supposed to mean

blocks.text: The official name was the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution. Mao's May 16 Notification of 1966 claimed that representatives of the bourgeoisie had sneaked into the party, the government, the army and the cultural world, and that some of them were people of the Khrushchev type still nestling beside the leadership. The remedy was not a quiet purge by the security services. It was to mobilise the masses, especially the young, to expose and overthrow those "capitalist roaders".

items: Attack the Four Olds: old ideas, old culture, old customs and old habits. In practice this meant temple idols, classical books, family heirlooms, shop signs and anyone labelled a landlord, rightist or intellectual.
Bombard the headquarters: Mao's phrase for attacking the party and state organs that he said were practising a bourgeois dictatorship.
Rebellion is justified: a slogan that licensed students and workers to defy local party committees, form Red Guard and rebel groups, and seize power.
Mao Zedong Thought as the measure of everything: the Little Red Book, loyalty dances, and public struggle sessions in which victims had to confess political sins.
Revolutionary committees: new governing bodies supposed to unite rebels, old cadres and the army after power seizures. In many places they became arenas for factional war.

blocks.text: The stated goal was to prevent China from changing colour and to remake the minds of a generation. The immediate political goal was to destroy Liu Shaoqi's authority, purge Deng Xiaoping and other pragmatists, and restore Mao as the unchallenged centre of the system. Both goals produced chaos that Mao himself later had to stop with the army.

sections.title: Who drove it, who was destroyed, who tried to hold the centre

people.name: Mao Zedong
people.text: Chairman of the Chinese Communist Party. After the Great Leap he feared loss of power and "revisionism". He launched the Cultural Revolution, protected the Red Guards while they served his purposes, then used the army to crush them when factional war threatened the state. He died in September 1976 without naming a clear long-term successor.

people.name: Liu Shaoqi
people.text: State president and Mao's designated successor until 1966. He and Deng Xiaoping had managed the post-famine recovery. Denounced as the biggest capitalist roader, publicly humiliated, expelled from the party in 1968, and left to die of illness in custody in Kaifeng in November 1969. He was rehabilitated after Mao's death.

people.name: Lin Biao
people.text: Marshal and defence minister who built the cult of Mao inside the army and promoted the Little Red Book. Named Mao's successor at the Ninth Party Congress in 1969. After relations with Mao collapsed, he died in a plane crash in Mongolia on 13 September 1971 while fleeing. The party later denounced him as a traitor.

people.name: Jiang Qing
people.text: Mao's wife and a leading figure in the Cultural Revolution Group. She dominated radical cultural policy, promoted model revolutionary operas, and attacked artists and officials. Arrested with the Gang of Four in October 1976, sentenced, and died by suicide in prison in 1991.

people.name: Zhou Enlai
people.text: Premier throughout the period. He protected some scientists, diplomats and cultural figures, negotiated with foreign visitors, and tried to keep the government functioning. Public mourning after his death in January 1976 turned into protests against the radicals.

people.name: Deng Xiaoping
people.text: Purged early as Liu's ally, brought back by Mao in 1973 to help run the economy, purged again after the April 1976 Tiananmen protests, then returned after Mao's death to become the architect of reform and opening. His later verdict kept Mao's portrait while condemning the Cultural Revolution.

sections.title: From big-character posters to army rule

blocks.text: The opening move was bureaucratic. On 16 May 1966 the Central Committee issued the May 16 Notification, dissolved Peng Zhen's Five Man Group that had tried to keep the campaign inside cultural debate, and created a new Cultural Revolution Group answerable to Mao's allies. Within days a dazibao at Peking University, written by Nie Yuanzi and colleagues, was broadcast across the country. Work teams sent by Liu and Deng to control campus unrest only made Mao more determined.

On 5 August Mao posted "Bombard the Headquarters". The Eleventh Plenum of the Eighth Central Committee rewrote the hierarchy: Lin Biao rose; Liu Shaoqi fell. Red Guard groups, often named after schools or factories, spread from Beijing. In August and September 1966 — later called Red August in the capital — teachers were beaten, homes of people with landlord or rightist labels were ransacked, and temples and classical artefacts were destroyed as Four Olds. Mao reviewed waves of Red Guards in Tiananmen Square and told them that rebellion was justified.

In January 1967 rebels seized power in Shanghai. Similar seizures followed elsewhere. Old party committees were replaced by revolutionary committees that were supposed to unite rebels, cadres and soldiers. Instead, rival rebel factions fought for control of cities, factories and even arsenals. In 1967 and 1968 China came close to civil war inside a still-standing party state. Mao authorised the People's Liberation Army to "support the left", which in practice meant picking winners and suppressing losers. By late 1968 most independent Red Guard organisations were finished.

The next phase was quieter and longer. From late 1968 the state sent urban secondary-school and university graduates "up to the mountains and down to the countryside". Roughly seventeen million young people were relocated over the following years. Officially they were to learn from poor and lower-middle peasants. Many lost years of education; some never returned to the cities. In the countryside, as Walder and Su later showed from county annals, the deadliest years were often 1968 to 1971, when military-backed authorities ran investigation campaigns, struggle sessions and executions after the street fighting had already been stopped.

Lin Biao's fall in 1971 shattered the myth that the Cultural Revolution followed a single clear line. The Ninth Congress had written him into the constitution as successor. Two years later he was dead in Mongolia and denounced. The Gang of Four — Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen — remained powerful in culture and propaganda, while Zhou Enlai and, briefly, Deng Xiaoping tried to stabilise the economy and diplomacy. Nixon's 1972 visit showed that Mao could open to the United States even while China remained in political turmoil at home.

sections.title: The Little Red Book that outprinted almost everything

blocks.text: Before the Cultural Revolution became a national upheaval, it had a pocket bible. In May 1964 the General Political Department of the People's Liberation Army issued Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung for soldiers. The first edition collected a few hundred short extracts under topical headings. Lin Biao's circle had already been printing a Mao quote in the army newspaper every day; the book made that practice portable.

Demand exploded once the Cultural Revolution began. Daniel Leese, who has studied the Mao cult in detail, estimates that official printings of the Quotations between 1966 and 1969 ran just over one billion copies inside China, not counting local reprints, foreign-language editions, army-internal versions, or handwritten and mimeographed collections. In 1966 alone more than 200 million copies were printed. Red vinyl covers, plastic wrappers and the ritual of waving the book at rallies made it the visual signature of the decade.

The book mattered because it turned politics into a script anyone could recite. Struggle sessions, factory meetings and school assemblies quoted Mao at opponents. After Lin Biao's death his preface was stripped from later printings, a reminder that even the sacred text was a weapon inside elite conflict. The physical object outlasted the man who had done most to promote it.

sections.title: While China turned inward, 1968 shook other capitals

blocks.text: The Cultural Revolution overlapped with a worldwide year of revolt, but the directions were different. In Czechoslovakia, Alexander Dubček's Prague Spring tried to loosen censorship and introduce "socialism with a human face". In August 1968 Warsaw Pact tanks crushed that experiment. Mao's China denounced Soviet "revisionism" and condemned the invasion as great-power bullying, while at home the army was already being used to end Red Guard anarchy. Reform from below in Prague and radicalisation from above in Beijing were not the same project.

In Western Europe and the United States, 1968 meant student occupations, anti-war marches and New Left fascination with Maoist slogans. Some activists waved Little Red Books without living under a state that could send them to the countryside or put them through struggle sessions. In Cambodia, a few years later, the Khmer Rouge would push agrarian ultra-collectivism even further than Mao's China, with catastrophic results; their leaders had studied in Paris and looked to both Stalin and Mao as models.

On Taiwan, still under Kuomintang martial law, the Cultural Revolution was propaganda proof that Communist China destroyed culture and killed its own. Writers and students watched from across the Strait while Taiwan's own White Terror continued. The scar literature that appeared on the mainland after 1977, and the nativist literature debate in Taiwan in the same years, both grew out of societies asking what political violence had done to ordinary people — but under opposite regimes.

sections.title: Arrests, a verdict, and a past that is still hard to teach

blocks.text: Mao died on 9 September 1976. On 6 October Hua Guofeng, with support from senior military figures including Ye Jianying, arrested Jiang Qing and her three closest allies. The radical centre of the Cultural Revolution was gone within a month of Mao's death. Trials of the Gang of Four followed. Deng Xiaoping returned to power and, from late 1978, shifted China toward market reforms and opening to the outside world.

In June 1981 the party issued its historical resolution. It called the Cultural Revolution a comprehensive, prolonged and severe blunder, held Mao chiefly responsible, and still described Mao as a great Marxist and the principal founder of the People's Republic. That formula — keep the founder, condemn the decade — remains the official line. Public museums and school textbooks treat the period briefly. Independent research, oral history and overseas scholarship have filled in local death counts, factional wars and personal testimonies that the official narrative leaves thin.

The human consequences outlasted the politics. Families broken by struggle sessions, careers ended by class labels, and a generation of sent-down youth shaped Chinese society into the reform era. The party that Mao nearly wrecked survived by restoring hierarchy, rehabilitating many victims, and forbidding any new mass movement of that kind — while retaining Mao's portrait on Tiananmen Gate.

sections.title: If Mao feared the party had gone soft, why did unleashing the masses almost destroy the party he needed?

blocks.text: Mao launched the Cultural Revolution because he believed the Communist Party apparatus was sliding toward Soviet-style revisionism and blocking his line. Yet the tools he chose — student and worker rebellion, public humiliation of cadres, dual power in the streets — disabled the very organisation that kept the country governable, until he had to bring the army back in. Was the Cultural Revolution a failed attempt to renew revolution from below, or a palace war that used society as its battlefield and then had to put society back in its place?

fun_fact.title: A billion pocket books
fun_fact.text: Daniel Leese estimates that official Chinese printings of Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung between 1966 and 1969 alone ran just over one billion copies — before counting local editions, translations, army-only printings, or handmade versions. In print-run terms it rivals the modern Bible, yet most copies were produced in only a few years for a single political campaign.

glossary.explain: The political and social upheaval Mao launched in 1966 and that ended after his death with the arrest of the Gang of Four in October 1976.
1893–1976. Chairman of the Chinese Communist Party and the dominant leader of the People's Republic from 1949 until his death.
Mao's 1958–1962 crash campaign of communes and backyard industry, which caused a famine that killed tens of millions.
1898–1969. State president and Mao's successor-designate until the Cultural Revolution; purged, expelled from the party, and died in custody.
1904–1997. Senior leader purged twice in the Cultural Revolution; later the chief architect of China's reform and opening.
1907–1971. Defence minister who promoted the Mao cult and the Little Red Book; named successor in 1969; died in a plane crash in Mongolia in 1971.
1914–1991. Mao's wife; leading Cultural Revolution radical in culture and propaganda; arrested as part of the Gang of Four.
1898–1976. Premier of China throughout the Cultural Revolution; tried to keep the state running and protect some specialists.
Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen; radical leaders arrested on 6 October 1976.
1921–2008. Mao's short-term successor as party chairman; with military allies he ordered the arrest of the Gang of Four.
The Central Committee body set up in May 1966 to direct the movement; included Chen Boda, Jiang Qing, Kang Sheng and other radicals.
The 1966 Central Committee circular that dissolved the Five Man Group and formally launched the Cultural Revolution.
Mao's 5 August 1966 big-character poster calling for attacks on the "bourgeois" party leadership, aimed especially at Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping.
Student and youth groups mobilised in 1966–68 to attack the Four Olds, teachers, officials and rival factions.
Old ideas, old culture, old customs and old habits — the categories Red Guards were told to smash.
Large handwritten political posters pasted on walls; a main medium of accusation and mobilisation in 1966–67.
Philosophy instructor at Peking University whose May 1966 dazibao helped ignite campus rebellion.
August–September 1966 in Beijing, when Red Guard violence, killings and Four Olds attacks surged after Mao's reviews.
January 1967 seizure of municipal power in Shanghai by rebels, which became a model for power seizures elsewhere.
Governing bodies formed after 1967 power seizures, supposedly uniting rebels, cadres and the army.
China's military; ordered to restore order in 1967–68 and central to ending Red Guard factional war.

glossary.term: Up to the Mountains and Down to the Countryside
glossary.explain: Campaign, peaking from 1968, that sent about 17 million urban youths to rural areas for re-education through labour.
Pocket anthology of Mao quotations first issued by the PLA in 1964; printed in vast numbers during the Cultural Revolution.
The official label for Mao's ideas as the ideological standard during the campaign.
Label for party leaders accused of taking China toward capitalism; applied above all to Liu Shaoqi.
Mao's charge against Soviet leaders after Stalin, and against Chinese colleagues he said were following the same path.
Public meetings where victims were forced to confess political crimes, often with humiliation and violence.
April 1969 Communist Party congress that wrote Lin Biao into the constitution as Mao's successor.
April 1976 gatherings in Tiananmen Square mourning Zhou Enlai and criticising the radicals; used as a pretext to purge Deng again.
The Communist Party's 1981 verdict condemning the Cultural Revolution while affirming Mao's overall historical role.
Stanford sociologist who, with Yang Su and others, estimated Cultural Revolution deaths from local annals.
Sociologist who co-authored major quantitative studies of Cultural Revolution violence in the countryside.
Historian of the Mao cult; estimated official Little Red Book print runs in the late 1960s.
1968 reform movement in Czechoslovakia crushed by Warsaw Pact invasion in August; contemporary with the Cultural Revolution but opposite in aim.
Cambodian communist movement that took power in 1975 and imposed radical agrarian policies influenced in part by Maoist models.
Post-1977 Chinese fiction about suffering in the Cultural Revolution; named after Lu Xinhua's story "Scar".
Beijing party boss who headed the Five Man Group; purged at the start of the Cultural Revolution.
Mao's former secretary; headed the Cultural Revolution Group in its early phase.
Shanghai radical and Gang of Four member, central to the January 1967 power seizure.
Literary critic and Gang of Four member; his 1965 attack on a play helped open the cultural offensive.
Shanghai worker-rebel elevated to national leadership; youngest member of the Gang of Four.
Marshal who helped Hua Guofeng arrest the Gang of Four in October 1976.
Soviet leader whose de-Stalinisation Mao treated as the model of revisionism China must avoid.
U.S. president who visited Beijing in February 1972 during the Cultural Revolution.
